newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Shrinking market share to hurt HK Telecom 96 net.
newsitem.headline: Shrinking market share to hurt HK Telecom 96 net.

text.p: Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd is expected to unveil a picture of shrinking market share and cut-throat competition when it reveals profits for the year to March 31 on Thursday, analysts said.

Once a traditional widows and orphans stock, thanks to its fat margins, monopoly status and affluent captive market, Hongkong Telecom has had to face the chill winds of competition from nimbler and smaller rivals in the past year.

"I'm expecting a profit of HK$10.8 billion, and an EPS (earnings per share) of HK$0.937," said Philip Wickham of G.K. Goh Securities, who predicted profits for the year to March 1998 of HK$12.2 billion and EPS of HK$1.30.
This would be 8.7 percent higher than the utility's previous result of HK$9.94 billion for the year to March 1996.
"It's not exciting growth at all," Wickham told Reuters.
Analysts said competition for international direct dial (IDD) business had eroded its market share and margins.
It has lost its monopoly on domestic calls, and although its monopoly on international calls does not expire until 2006, competitors are already making inroads through callback systems.
Call-back systems involve bypassing high tariff rates by allowing a call from a high-tariff country to be made to a "callback switch" in another lower-tariff country.
The call-back switch initiates the call, and the customer pays a lower fee to the call-back carrier.
Since July 1995, Wharf Holdings Ltd's New T&T, New World Development Co Ltd's New World Telecom and Hutchison Whampoa Ltd's Hutchison Telecom have competed with Hongkong Telecom on domestic services.
Hongkong Telecom hit back at call-back operators in April by offering its own cut-price IDD services -- "IDD 001 Savings Plan" and an "0060 International Call Service".
But Wickham estimates it has lost an average 20 percent of the international market in the year to March, 1997, leaving it with 80 percent of the market.
Using a "spot rate" calculation -- its market share on a given day such as March 31 -- the utility's share could have fallen as low as 70-75 percent, Wickham said.
Lloyd Fischer, BZW Asia's head of regional telecommunications research, estimated that Hongkong Telecom's spot market share at March 31 could be as low as 65 percent.
Fischer has forecast net profit for Hongkong Telecom of HK$11.077 billion for the year to March.
Salomon Brothers analyst Dan Sherman expects Hongkong Telecom to report net profit of HK$11.15 billion, rising to HK$12.50 billion for the year to March 1998.
SBC Warburg analyst Jason Billings had a lower forecast for the utility, predicting net profit of HK$10.96 billion.
Billings said Hongkong Telecom actually compared very well to other telecom monopolies in the region in terms of adapting to a changing regulatory environment and tougher competition.

"We believe they are doing the best they can, given the upcoming circumstances of the political effects of the handover, change of regulatory structure -- i.e. liberalisation -- local and international competition ... and technological challenges," Billings said.
